analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill to replace all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax drew 75 cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, dying quietly in the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Tax would have wiped out the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate tax, and replaced them with a single 23% national sales tax on almost everything people buy, collected mostly by the states, with the IRS shut down. Every family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. Because the tax falls on spending rather than income, and because investment purchases would be exempt, households that earn and hold the most money would pay the least, while working families that spend most of their paychecks would bear the full rate. The bill was introduced on the first day of the 113th Congress with 75 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received so much as a committee hearing before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with the greatest wealth and income gain the most: the estate tax disappears entirely, and income from capital gains, dividends, and interest would go untaxed, since investment purchases are exempt from the sales tax. Savers and businesses gain from the investment and business exemptions. Low-income families gain some protection through the monthly rebate that covers the tax on poverty-level spending, and every worker's paycheck rises with the end of payroll tax withholding. The tax preparation industry, by contrast, loses its market.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, ending annual income tax filing and raising take-home pay by removing payroll deductions.
It gives every family a monthly cash rebate equal to the sales tax on spending up to the federal poverty level, so no family pays the tax on essential poverty-level consumption.
It abolishes the IRS by prohibiting its funding after fiscal year 2017, replacing federal tax administration largely with state agencies and new Treasury bureaus.
It exempts business, export, and investment purchases from the tax so that taxation falls once, on final consumption, rather than cascading through production.

analysis.who_pays: Working and middle-income families who spend most of what they earn. They would pay the full 23% on nearly every purchase — on top of their state's sales tax — while wealthier households, who save and invest much of their income, would pay the tax on only a fraction of their resources. Families above the poverty line get no rebate on spending beyond it, and the Social Security and Medicare trust funds would depend on the flow of general sales tax revenue instead of dedicated payroll contributions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income households that spend most of their pay

drawbacks.text: A 23% federal sales tax would be added on top of existing state sales taxes, raising the price of nearly everything families buy. Because families with middle incomes spend most of what they earn, while the wealthiest spend only a fraction and keep the rest untaxed, the effective tax rate would fall heaviest on working and middle-class households.

Purchases made for investment purposes are expressly exempt from the tax, so income from wealth — capital gains, dividends, interest — would go entirely untaxed, while wages spent on rent, food, and cars would be taxed at the full rate.

Repealing the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare, and replacing that funding with a share of general sales tax revenue, ends the dedicated link between contributions and benefits and makes those programs dependent on yearly sales tax collections.

The prebate only offsets the tax on poverty-level spending; it requires every family to register annually with the government, listing Social Security numbers and certifying residency for each member, to keep receiving it.

The sales tax is set to expire seven years after enactment unless the Sixteenth Amendment — the constitutional amendment allowing the income tax — is repealed by the states, a hurdle no tax proposal has ever cleared, leaving the whole plan contingent on an unlikely constitutional process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification case is real: a single visible sales tax, no annual filings, no IRS, and a rebate that shields poverty-level spending would end a genuinely burdensome compliance system. But the costs are large and land unevenly. The plan shifts taxation from income and wealth to consumption, which systematically favors households that live off savings and assets and raises the effective tax rate on working families who spend most of what they earn. Repealing the estate tax removes the only federal tax on very large inheritances, and repealing payroll taxes breaks the dedicated funding link for Social Security and Medicare, replacing it with annual appropriations from a consumption tax. The prebate softens but does not eliminate the regressivity, because it only offsets the tax on poverty-level spending — every dollar of consumption above that line is taxed at the full rate regardless of whether the spender earns $40,000 or $4 million. An honest reading is that the bill trades real administrative relief for a substantial redistribution of the tax burden toward the middle class and away from concentrated wealth.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on the first day of the new Congress, sent to the tax-writing committee, and never heard from again — no hearing, no markup, no vote — until the Congress expired two years later.

narrative.text: Rep. Rob Woodall introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2013 on January 3, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
Seventy-five House members signed on as cosponsors, all of them Republicans.
The action history shows only two entries — introduction and committee referral — with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote at any point before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill would have repealed the income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, imposed a 23% national sales tax starting in 2015, and prohibited funding the IRS after fiscal year 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax system and the interests that fare well under it: the tax preparation industry keeps its market, and wealthy households continue to pay estate and capital income taxes that the bill would have erased. Middle-income taxpayers keep the current tax structure rather than the consumption-tax burden the bill would have shifted onto them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing tax code and the tax-prep industry

sides.party_line_note: All 75 cosponsors were Republicans and none was a Democrat; the Republican chairman of the tax-writing committee nevertheless never moved the bill, so it never came to a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax and the income tax on capital gains, dividends, and interest, while exempting investment purchases from the sales tax. The 23% consumption tax would be borne mainly by households that spend most of their income, so the net effect is a large transfer of tax burden away from the wealthiest families onto wage earners.

Property purchased for investment is exempt from the tax, and intangibles like securities and bonds are not taxable, so returns on wealth would go untaxed. This would make saving through financial assets permanently more favorable relative to wages.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax compliance industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax eliminates the annual filing obligation that supports tax preparers, tax software companies, and much of the tax advisory business. Consumers would keep the money they now spend on filing, so the industry's loss is the public's simplification gain.

Sellers would have to collect, report, and remit a 23% federal tax monthly, post large security bonds if they are big sellers, and face penalties for failures. In exchange they receive an administration credit of the greater of $200 or a quarter of one percent of tax remitted, compensating only part of the compliance burden.

States that agree to collect the federal tax would keep an administration fee of a quarter of one percent of collections, making state agencies the permanent collection channel for the federal sales tax.

The bill prohibits funding the IRS after fiscal year 2017 and replaces it with an Excise Tax Bureau and a Sales Tax Bureau plus state administrators. Its elimination is the headline simplification the bill promises to taxpayers.
